The posts, the census and the district Special Branch sections stand, and the historical police has caught up with them in size; what the Republic keeps from 1964 is the chiefs' experience and four extra years of files.
> 
> The radar's ledger has made the interdiction debate honest and changed nothing it was about: the Trail is larger at the end of 1971 than ever, the Liberation Route through northeastern Cambodia is mapped and open, and the aircraft that count both will leave with the Americans¹³.
> 
> The ARVN's I Corps ends the phase believing, on the evidence of Lolo and Sophia, that a besieged base under American bombers holds. It is true, and it is the belief that will cost it most when the bombers go¹⁶.
> 
> Phung Hoang ends 1971 with an audited count of about 63,000 neutralized since 1965 and a national file of about 230,000 names in one building in Saigon, serving the President as well as the war. About 3,500 selected advisers remain, with the territorials and the province teams more than with the divisions; the American battalions have gone home whole and their discipline has decayed on its historical course⁶.
> 
> The board ends 1971 as the machinery of the army below colonel and nothing above it: battalions and regiments are commanded by officers it chose, for terms it sets, and the divisions and corps by the President's choices⁷. The colonels who asked for the list back are in the schools and the staffs. The battalions that went into Laos came out of it better than the operation did.

### New: The closed loop
*1 Jul 1969 – 31 Dec 1971 · The Bien Hoa rebuild works and the Go Vap signal depot; the ARVN depots at Long Binh and Da Nang; the 1st and 3rd Area Logistics Commands · EV008-6*

*Initiative: allied*

Vietnamization handed the RVNAF the equipment of an American army in three years, and in this war the Republic already had the shops to keep it running. From the summer of 1969 the departing American units turned in their vehicles, radios and weapons for transfer, and the Bien Hoa rebuild works and the Go Vap signal depot, which had rebuilt the RVNAF's own engines, carriers and sets at the domestic share since 1966, took the American articles into the same loop: in 1970 the works rebuilt about 4,500 engines, 2,000 transmissions and about 550 M113s and M41s, and the depot about 45,000 radios, most of them PRC-25s and PRC-77s, which the communications plant had built under licence since 1969. The crash depot programme that the historical RVNAF needed in 1970–71, when it found itself owning more equipment than it could repair, did not have to be built, and the American logistics staff that would have built it spent the time on the ports⁹⁸.

The loop was tested in the spring of 1971. Lam Son 719 lost about a third of the 1st Armored Brigade's carriers and tanks in Laos, most of them abandoned on Route 9 where no rebuild works could reach them. Of those that came back damaged, the works at Da Nang and Bien Hoa returned about 60 to the brigade by August, and its squadrons were at about four-fifths of their establishment again by the end of the year⁸. The brigade's losses in Laos were history's, and the reason was the operation, not the depot. What the depot changed was how long it took to stand the brigade up again.

By the end of 1971 about two-fifths of the RVNAF's small-arms cartridge cases, about a third of its 105mm bodies, most of its mortar bodies, most of its radio batteries and all of its field wire came from its own plants, filled and powered with American propellant, explosive and semiconductors bought with aid dollars. It was the largest step toward a self-supplying army the Republic ever took, and in 1971 nobody could see it, because the American stocks were still free and still flowing. The Joint General Staff's J-4, which in 1970 would historically have been absorbed by the turnover, spent part of that year drafting the first plan for an RVNAF that would buy its own ammunition with its own money; it was filed and not funded⁸.

### New: The Board and the Directorate in the palace
*Jan 1970 – Sep 1971 · Saigon and the provinces · EV002-6*

*Initiative: allied*
The Provincial Administration Selection Board had outlived four governments because each had found it cheaper to keep than to break, and because a province chief appointed outside the list could not sign a budget, a title or a counterpart-fund disbursement while the Aid Compliance Board stood behind the rule¹⁰. By 1970 the American lever was lapsing with the withdrawal, and Thieu, preparing for the election of 1971, wanted the provinces. He did not abolish the Board. As the terms of its two general officers expired in January 1970 he replaced them with officers of his own staff, and from that spring his Prime Minister, General Tran Thien Khiem, appointed the third name on the list for about half the province vacancies and for most of those in the provinces with the largest electorates. The list still excluded the incompetent and the bought; it no longer excluded the loyal mediocre³.

The Inspectorate's reports, which had gone to the Board and the Commission since 1964, were routed through the presidential Inspectorate General from July 1971 under the decree that subordinated the Commission. The National Police had followed the same road earlier: its Director General had been the President's appointee in fact since 1966, and in 1970–71 the Special Branch's Saigon headquarters spent a growing share of its effort on the opposition, the An Quang Buddhists and the Ky camp, as historical police chiefs always had. The rural posts, the census and the district sections went on much as before, because they were too many and too local for the palace to want them. In September 1971 province chiefs campaigned for Thieu as they did on the historical course; the difference was that about two-thirds of them were men who had passed an examination and served a district first, and the villages they governed were governed better than they were represented³.

The palace took Phung Hoang's national file the same way, without abolishing anything. In February 1970 Khiem, who was Minister of the Interior as well as Prime Minister, moved the national centre from the Directorate of National Police to the Central Intelligence Organization's building and replaced Hieu, who resigned rather than serve under the new chairman, with a Military Security colonel of the President's staff. The file held about 210,000 names by then, every one entered to the three-source standard and many with fingerprints and photographs, and it now served a second purpose: from the spring of 1970 the national centre vetted every candidate for province and district office and every officer above major against it, and its analysts were asked to chart the An Quang Buddhists' committees and the Ky camp's officers by the same method they had used on the Front. For the election of 1971 the provincial copies of the file were called in to Saigon "for consolidation", and about two-thirds of the PIOCCs were left with district extracts; from September 1971 the complete national file existed in one building. Ashby's successor protested in writing in October 1970 and was told, correctly, that the decree of 1964 placed the committee under the Minister of the Interior⁶. The district centres went on working the Front as before, and their audited count did not fall; what had changed was who else the file was for.

The Directorate of Defence Industry went the same way in the same months, and for the same reason. In February 1970, as the Aid Compliance Board was reduced to an office reporting to the Embassy, Thieu replaced Vuong Dinh Toan with Brigadier General Vu Xuan Dac of his own military staff, and the Directorate's contracts, its scrap and import licences and its deferment list became the palace's to allot. The domestic share survived, because the Joint General Staff now wanted the plants for its own reasons and the Americans were leaving, and the lines ran as before. What did not survive was the acceptance the Phu Cat lot had made honest: from 1970 the proof-firing at Long Thanh was signed more often than fired, the share of lots rejected fell from about one in sixteen to about one in a hundred, and the field reports of duds and misfires from domestic mortar rounds roughly doubled by 1971. The scrap brass of the arsenal's case lines went to Singapore through a firm whose partners were related to the President's staff, and the Commission, under the Inspectorate from July 1971, could not open the file⁸.

Taken together, the five institutions this headquarters built behind an American lever in 1964 fell to that lever's lapse in eighteen months: the Commission, the Selection Board for the provinces, the general-officer list, the national Phung Hoang file and the Directorate⁸. Each lost its reach upward and kept its work below the palace, and the net is the same in each case. The posts, the chiefs' experience, the battalion commanders, the district centres and the plants' output stayed with the Republic; the honesty above them went to the palace. Of the five, the Directorate lost least in output and most in what output is worth.

### New: The handover of the call at Long My
*1 Feb 1970 – 30 Jun 1971 · Long My District, Chuong Thien Province; the Vi Thanh sector operations centre; the district's territorial artillery platoon · EV008-7*

*Initiative: allied*

When the Americans left the districts of the Delta, the call for help stayed behind, and Long My is the place to see it. Major Huynh Cong Tri, a list chief who had held the district since 1966, had forty-one PF posts and two Regional Force companies along the Cai Lon and the roads to Vi Thanh, every post with a set on the district net and every set made at Go Vap. Since 1967, under the rules that came out of Cai Lay, each post's first call had gone to a gun: until 1970 most often to an American battery or helicopter fire team through the subsector adviser's radio, and from February 1970 to the district's own two-gun 105mm territorial artillery platoon, formed that month on howitzers rebuilt at Bien Hoa and fed with Bien Hoa's rounds⁸.

Major Daniel R. Kearsley, the selected adviser who held the subsector from 1969, spent his last year handing the call over. Every post's concentrations were re-plotted for the district platoon and the 21st Division's guns at Vi Thanh; the post commanders called them in Vietnamese, on Vietnamese sets, to Vietnamese gunners, with Kearsley listening and not speaking; and from September 1970 the American fire teams were called only through the district operations room, at Tri's request. On the night of 23–24 February 1971, two months before Kearsley left, a company of the U Minh 10th Battalion came against the post at Xeo Mat at 0110; the post called at 0112, the district platoon fired its first round at 0117, and by 0140 it had put about sixty rounds on the post's three concentrations and the company had withdrawn, leaving four dead in the canal⁸. Nobody in the chain was American.

The handover worked because what it handed over was Vietnamese at both ends: the set, the battery, the gun and the round. It did not work for anything that had been American at one end. The B-52Js and the coordinate cell that had broken the sieges of the larger war were not handed to anyone, and no district could call them. When the advisers left Long My in June 1971, the district kept every post it had and the Front kept the canal at night between them, as it had before⁸. Tri's returns, which kept all forty-one posts through the offensive of 1972, began in that handover.

## Phase VI — Paris, the endgame, and 1975 (Jan 1973 – Dec 1975)

### Overview (changed)

Phase VI is the war without the Americans, and the end of the Republic of Vietnam. The Paris Agreement of January 1973 takes US forces out and returns the prisoners; it leaves the PAVN in the South, the Thieu government in Saigon, and the war to be decided between them. The ceasefire never holds. In 1973 Saigon is on the offensive, recovering hamlets and roads, while the North rebuilds; in 1974 the two are evenly matched, and the ARVN, short of ammunition, fuel and spare parts as American aid falls, bleeds in a war of attrition it cannot sustain; in January 1975 the North tests whether the United States will respond to the seizure of a province, and when it does not, it commits everything¹⁷.

The shape of the phase is three slow years and seven fast weeks. The constraints that bind the American role are now law, not policy: the Case–Church amendment ends all US combat activity in Indochina from 15 August 1973, the War Powers Resolution limits the President's power to send forces back, and Congress cuts military aid. Watergate removes the President who gave Thieu his assurances. In Hanoi, the 21st Plenum of October 1973 returns to revolutionary violence, and the PAVN builds a road network east of the mountains, a fuel pipeline into the South and an army of corps. In Saigon, the economy, hit by the oil shock and the departure of the Americans whose spending had sustained it, and a government that has narrowed its base, face the offensive of 1975 with an army spread thin across the whole country. When the blow falls at Ban Me Thuot in March, Thieu's decision to abandon the Highlands turns a defeat into a rout, and in eight weeks the Republic falls. The PAVN enters Saigon on 30 April 1975.

In this war the army that fights the last three years has been built for ten years around the belt-fed gun and the abundance of American ammunition, and the ration of 1974 finds it more dependent on volume than the historical one. It fights the attrition of 1974 and the stand at Xuan Loc with better weapons than its enemy and too few rounds to use them, and the hoards it builds against the ration are lost with I Corps.

The bombers leave in August 1973 without bombing Neak Luong, and the coordinate cell is disbanded with nothing in the VNAF to send coordinates to. The ARVN fights 1974 and the defence of Phuoc Long with plans written for an air force that no longer comes, and loses Thuong Duc and Phuoc Long as history did, with its officers knowing exactly what they lack.

Phung Hoang outlives the Americans as a Vietnamese programme and helps the Republic's offensive of 1973 in the Delta; its national file, consolidated in Saigon since 1971, is taken intact on 30 April 1975 with the files of Da Nang a month earlier, and it serves the victors' security service as the most complete list of their enemies they will ever hold. The advisers are gone in March 1973, and nothing of their eighteen months survives them but the counterparts who remember them, who are on the lists.

The officer reforms leave the Republic in its last three years an officer corps that knows precisely what it lacks. Its battalion and regimental commanders, educated on a doctrine built around American fire, plan the battles of 1974 for a weight of fire the ration no longer allows. Its staff college writes, in November 1974, the only serious plan the Republic ever had for a defence on reduced resources, and the President takes its conclusion and not its method in March 1975. At Xuan Loc a well-led division holds for twelve days, as history's did. Saigon falls on 30 April.

In this war the last ration also fell on an army that made two-fifths of its own small-arms ammunition, a third of its 105mm rounds and nearly all of its radio batteries, from imported powder and semiconductors. The $700 million of fiscal 1975 bought about what $850 million to $1 billion bought historically; the squad gun's ration roughly doubled from March 1974, and the territorial posts' radios stayed on the air. It made the attrition of 1974 somewhat cheaper and changed no position the PAVN chose to take, gave Phuoc Long more rounds than it could fire, and reached none of the decisions of March 1975. On 30 April the 4th Corps took the plants intact, on orders.

### How the phase ends (changed)

The war ends on 30 April 1975 with the fall of Saigon and the unconditional surrender of the Republic of Vietnam. In this war that date is a conclusion and not an assumption: it was set in Hanoi by a resolution to finish before the rains and by the march of the 1st Corps, and the mechanisms in this war that pulled the fall later (the better battalions at Duc Duc, Xuan Loc, Phan Rang and Cu Chi, the PAVN's greener divisions, a stronger held belt in the Delta) acted on fights the PAVN chose to bypass, while those that pulled it earlier (a President more certain his army could not hold alone, an army more dependent on fire it no longer had) acted on decisions the palace took on the historical days for its own reasons¹⁸. Rung (a), collapse. The Paris Agreement had removed the American forces and kept the PAVN in the South; Congress had written the end of American combat and the limits on the President into law; American military aid had fallen; and the government in Saigon, more stable than at any time since 1963 but narrowly based, economically weakened and dependent on American supply, faced an enemy that had rebuilt after 1972 and chose its moment. The decisive blows were Hanoi's, at Phuoc Long and Ban Me Thuot; the decisive errors were Saigon's, in the order to abandon the Highlands and the contradictory orders to I Corps.

The Republic that met the offensive was not the historical Republic, and the end vector of this phase, measured after the fall, cannot show it. At the end of 1974, on the eve of Phuoc Long, the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region was held at night more firmly than history's, and the Front's district committees there had lost about twice the historical share of their members in 1973⁶; the Special Branch's knowledge of the infrastructure was still the better for its ten years of files; the government's standing in the hamlets was history's, after the decrees of 1972; the army's battalions were better led and its divisions and corps no better; and the army as a whole was more dependent than history's on American fire it no longer had, and knew it¹⁸. Every one of those differences was erased by the fall, and the vector returns to history because the state it measured no longer existed.

Hanoi's posture never changed. It was committed to armed reunification throughout, from the Ninth Plenum of December 1963 to the Ho Chi Minh Campaign, through the losses of 1965–68 and 1972, and it accepted the Paris Agreement as a step towards that end. The timing of its last campaign was its own, set by its army's road and the season. The US war in Vietnam, from the advisory years to 1973, cost more than 58,000 American dead. The Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, northern and southern, are counted in the millions by most estimates, and the record of them is less precise than the record of the Americans.

The squad guns and the marksmen's rifles of the ARVN, and about 9 million rounds of linked 5.56mm from the divisional hoards of I and II Corps, are in the PAVN's hands by the end of April 1975, with the carbines of a million men⁵.

The Republic's defence of every besieged town had been built since 1971 around American bombers and American coordinates, and both were gone by the end of 1973¹⁶.

The officers the reforms made fought the last campaign as well as any part of the RVNAF fought it, and their best staff plan was taken by the President and executed without its method. About 12,000 of the board's officers were captured in 1975 and sent to the re-education camps with the rest of the officer corps; the board's files, with the evaluation report of every officer since 1964, were in the Joint General Staff's compound on 30 April⁷.

The Republic's own plants stretched its last aid dollar by about a third to two-fifths and kept its radios on the air through 1974; they shortened no collapse, because the collapse of March 1975 was decided by orders, families and an enemy who chose his ground, and they passed intact to the victors on 30 April⁸.

### Changed: The aid cuts and the shortages
*25 Jan – 9 Aug 1974 · South Vietnam and Washington · EV000-89*

*Initiative: neither*

On 25 January 1974 supplies of ammunition and fuel to all ARVN units were cut because of budget limits. US military aid fell from about $1.1 billion in fiscal year 1974 to an appropriation of about $700 million for fiscal year 1975, the July 1974–June 1975 year, the figure given by source as $700–750 million¹⁷. Major General Murray of the Defense Attaché Office warned that cuts in support could roughly be equated with loss of territory, and that aid of $600 million would mean writing the South off¹⁹. The ARVN rationed artillery rounds, grounded aircraft and helicopters for lack of fuel and parts, and cut patrols; the soldiers' pay lost most of its value to inflation, and desertion rose. The economy suffered from the world oil shock of late 1973 and the loss of American spending.

In this war the ration fell on an army that had been built for ten years around the belt-fed gun and the 30-round magazine, four years longer than the historical one. The Joint General Staff's directive of February 1974 limited each infantry squad to its basic load for a month's operations, and the squad gun went first: about 200 rounds a gun for a month, which is what an M249 fires at the rapid rate in two minutes. Battalion commanders who had learned their trade breaking contacts with the squad gun's volume found that the 1974 ration let them do it about twice in a month, and the advisers' successors at the Defense Attaché Office reported that the infantry, rather than fight with aimed rifle fire as their fathers had fought with the Garand, avoided contacts it could not break with volume. The marksmen, whose match 7.62mm had a separate line, were rationed harder still; by the summer about half the M110A2s in I and II Corps were in arms rooms for want of ammunition. Divisions began to hoard linked 5.56mm in their own ammunition points against the ration, against JGS orders, and by the end of the year the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Divisions held about 9 million rounds outside the corps depots between them⁵. On 9 August 1974 Nixon resigned over Watergate, and Gerald Ford succeeded him¹⁹. The President who had given Thieu written promises was gone.

That was the ration on American stocks, and in this war it was not the whole of the ration. Since 1965 the Aid Compliance Board's domestic share had made the RVNAF buy from its own plants, and by 1974 the Bien Hoa arsenal made about two-fifths of the RVNAF's 5.56mm and 7.62mm cartridges, about a third of its 105mm rounds and most of its mortar rounds, every one of them filled with imported propellant and explosive bought out of the same $700 million. A dollar of propellant, primers and explosive loaded at Bien Hoa bought about one and a half times the rounds of a dollar of finished American ammunition, and the battery works and the signal depot stretched the communications dollar about twice⁹. Across the whole of the RVNAF's programme the fiscal 1975 appropriation bought about what $850 million to $1 billion had bought on the historical course. From March 1974 the Joint General Staff raised the squad gun's monthly ration to about 400 rounds and the 105mm battery's daily allowance by about a third, and the PRC-25 and PRC-77 batteries that the historical RVNAF rationed through 1974 were issued at the full rate from Go Vap; the territorial posts' radios, which history's district chiefs found going silent in the second half of the year, stayed on the air⁸.

The stretch did not reach fuel, aircraft or anything else imported whole. The VNAF grounded its aircraft and helicopters for want of fuel and parts on the historical scale, the 175mm and 155mm guns were rationed as before because Bien Hoa could not forge their bodies, and the thermal station at Thu Duc paid the oil shock's price for its fuel oil like every other plant in the country. Nor did it change the vote. In the House debate of the summer the arsenal was cited by the advocates of the cut as proof that the Republic could make its own ammunition, which was half true, since it made the brass and the steel and not the powder⁸. The appropriation was $700 million, as it was historically.

The plants also paid wages, and in 1974 that mattered in the households of the army. About 60,000–80,000 people worked in the Bien Hoa, Thu Duc and Go Vap works, more than half of them women on the battery and assembly lines, and perhaps one ARVN or RF family in eight in the provinces of III Corps had a factory wage in it. A private's pay in 1974 bought a fraction of what it had bought in 1971; a wife's wage at the battery works roughly doubled what the household had. The factory families of Bien Hoa were the one part of the army's families that the inflation of 1974 did not reach in full, and they lived beside the plants, not beside the units. Rice was the other side of the household: the pumps the agricultural machinery shops had sold since 1964 had put a dry-season crop on about 300,000 hectares of the held Delta by 1974, and the Delta's surplus that reached Saigon in 1974 was somewhat larger than history's, which held the price of rice in the capital a little below history's in a year when everything else rose⁸.

**Before:**

> On 25 January 1974 supplies of ammunition and fuel to all ARVN units were cut because of budget limits. US military aid fell from about $1.1 billion in fiscal year 1974 to an appropriation of about $700 million for fiscal year 1975, the July 1974–June 1975 year, the figure given by source as $700–750 million¹⁷. Major General Murray of the Defense Attaché Office warned that cuts in support could roughly be equated with loss of territory, and that aid of $600 million would mean writing the South off. The ARVN rationed artillery rounds, grounded aircraft and helicopters for lack of fuel and parts, and cut patrols; the soldiers' pay lost most of its value to inflation, and desertion rose. The economy suffered from the world oil shock of late 1973 and the loss of American spending.
> 
> In this war the ration fell on an army that had been built for ten years around the belt-fed gun and the 30-round magazine, four years longer than the historical one. The Joint General Staff's directive of February 1974 limited each infantry squad to its basic load for a month's operations, and the squad gun went first: about 200 rounds a gun for a month, which is what an M249 fires at the rapid rate in two minutes. Battalion commanders who had learned their trade breaking contacts with the squad gun's volume found that the 1974 ration let them do it about twice in a month, and the advisers' successors at the Defense Attaché Office reported that the infantry, rather than fight with aimed rifle fire as their fathers had fought with the Garand, avoided contacts it could not break with volume. The marksmen, whose match 7.62mm had a separate line, were rationed harder still; by the summer about half the M110A2s in I and II Corps were in arms rooms for want of ammunition. Divisions began to hoard linked 5.56mm in their own ammunition points against the ration, against JGS orders, and by the end of the year the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Divisions held about 9 million rounds outside the corps depots between them⁵. On 9 August 1974 Nixon resigned over Watergate, and Gerald Ford succeeded him¹⁹. The President who had given Thieu written promises was gone.

### Changed: The war of attrition of 1974
*16 May – 10 Dec 1974 · The Iron Triangle; Thuong Duc, Duc Duc and Phu Loc in I Corps · EV000-91*

*Initiative: enemy*

From May 1974 the PAVN took the initiative with a series of "strategic raids" designed to grind down the ARVN and test its reserves. In III Corps the PAVN 9th Division attacked Rach Bap in the Iron Triangle from 16 May; the ARVN retook it only in November. In I Corps a PAVN regiment overran An Hoa and attacked the district town of Thuong Duc from 18 July; the Airborne Division held the heights around it in a costly victory that lasted until November. At Duc Duc, from 18 July to 4 October, the ARVN 3rd Division suffered 4,700 casualties. From 28 August to 10 December the PAVN seized hills near Phu Loc that closed Phu Bai airfield to traffic and cut Highway 1, and the ARVN recovered them at heavy cost. In 1974 South Vietnam lost about 30,000 killed; the US estimated about 61,000 PAVN and VC killed¹⁹.

The weapons the ARVN carried in these fights were better than the PAVN's, as they had been since 1964, and it mattered less than at any time since. On the ridges west of Thuong Duc in September the 1st and 2nd Airborne Brigades took and retook Hill 1062 against the PAVN 304th Division's 66th Regiment; the Airborne's marksmen killed the 66th's spotters and gunners on the facing slopes at 500–700 metres, and its squads held the crest against three night assaults with the squad guns rationed to a belt each for the night. They held, and they bled, because the PAVN's 130mm guns and 122mm rockets were not rationed and the ARVN's 105s and 155s were⁵.

They bled in a second way that history's Airborne did not. Since An Loc, Kontum and the Lam Son bases the ARVN's I Corps had been taught, by success, to hold a besieged position and let the bombs break the siege. At Thuong Duc the district town's garrison, the 79th Ranger Battalion, dug in and waited, as its officers had seen the 23rd Division wait at Kontum, for a siege box that no longer existed; the 304th Division's regiment dug its trenches to the wire in eleven days without a bomb falling on them, and the town fell on 7 August. The Airborne's counter-attack on the heights was planned by officers who had held Lolo and Sophia in 1971 under the Js, and its first assaults on Hill 1062 went forward in the expectation that the PAVN's positions on the crest would be broken from the air first; the VNAF's A-37s and F-5As, flying in the monsoon cloud with unguided bombs, could not do it. I estimate that the Airborne Division's losses in the heights were perhaps a tenth higher than historically, a judgment I hold loosely, and I keep the 3rd Division's 4,700 at Duc Duc and South Vietnam's dead for the year at about 30,000¹⁹¹⁶. The ARVN, unable to replace its losses or its expended ammunition, had committed its strategic reserve, the Airborne and Marine Divisions, to static defence in I Corps, and had nothing left to move.

The officer reforms made the attrition of 1974 more legible and no cheaper. The battalion and regimental commanders who fought at Thuong Duc, Duc Duc and Phu Loc had been educated on a doctrine in which the infantry finds the enemy and the fires destroy him, and from January 1974 the fires were rationed; their reports to the Joint General Staff in the summer, collected by the Central Training Command, are the most exact account anywhere of what the ration did to each kind of fight, and none of them could change it. At Duc Duc the 3rd Division's battalions, under board commanders, held their companies together through 4,700 casualties with fewer men lost to desertion than history's, and held no more ground⁷. I keep South Vietnam's dead for the year at about 30,000¹⁹.

The Bien Hoa rounds changed which guns could fire, and the PAVN's choice of ground decided how much that was worth. Through the summer the 105mm batteries of the 3rd Division at Duc Duc and the Airborne on the Thuong Duc heights fired about a third more than the historical ration allowed, on domestic rounds, and every post and company on the ridges kept its radio on the air. It did not change the arithmetic of the artillery duel. The PAVN fought these battles where its 130mm M-46 guns, ranging 27 kilometres, could reach the ARVN's 105mm positions at 11 kilometres from beyond their range, and the guns the domestic rounds fed were the guns its choice of ground made least decisive. Thuong Duc still fell on 7 August, Duc Duc still cost the 3rd Division its 4,700, and Phu Loc was recovered in December as history's was; at Rach Bap the III Corps battalions, which drew directly from Bien Hoa, retook the post in the last week of October rather than in November. I judge that the domestic rounds and the radios saved perhaps 1,000–2,500 of the Republic's dead in 1974, resting on a third more 105mm fire and a doubled squad-gun ration in the fights the army did accept, and I keep the reported figure of about 30,000 dead for the year, since the saving lies inside its uncertainty¹⁹⁸. What absorbed the difference was the PAVN's choice of ground and the ARVN's lack of a reserve: a better-supplied army that could not move its divisions still lost the positions it was tied to.

### Changed: The fall of Phuoc Long
*12 Dec 1974 – 6 Jan 1975 · Phuoc Long Province (Phuoc Binh and Song Be), III Corps · EV000-92*

*Initiative: enemy*

On 12 December 1974 the PAVN 4th Corps under Hoang Cam, with the 7th Division, the new 3rd Division and independent regiments including the 141st, 165th, 201st and 271st, and two armoured companies with 14 T-54s, attacked Phuoc Long Province on the Cambodian border. It was defended mainly by Regional Force battalions, reinforced by the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 7th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 9th Regiment of the 5th Division and the 81st Airborne Ranger Battalion²⁰. The province chief's plan for the defence of Phuoc Binh, drafted in 1973 by officers who had served at An Loc, was a plan to hold the town for six to eight weeks while the bombers broke the siege; it named the bomber cells by the call signs Hollingsworth's men had used in 1972. On 13 December the province chief asked III Corps for "the B-52 support provided for in the plan", and III Corps forwarded the request to the Joint General Staff, which forwarded it to the Defense Attaché Office, which had no means to answer it¹⁶.

On 18 December, in the meeting at the Independence Palace where Thieu and the Joint General Staff decided not to send the general reserve to Phuoc Long, the request was on the table, and the decision taken was historical: the Airborne Division was committed in I Corps, and Thieu would not risk a second division in a province he judged he could not hold without American bombers. In this war the judgment was put in those words, and with more conviction, because the Republic's officers had seen at An Loc and Kontum what American bombers could do for a besieged town and knew exactly what they were not getting¹⁶. The last ARVN post fell on 6 January 1975, the first provincial capital lost permanently since the Paris Agreement. The ARVN lost more than 1,000 killed and 2,444 captured; the PAVN about 1,300 killed and wounded. Saigon did not try to retake it. Washington made no military response²⁰. In Hanoi, where a strategy conference sat from 18 December to 8 January, Phuoc Long answered the question the leadership had set itself: the United States would not return¹⁹. The plan for a two-year campaign to end the war in 1976 was adapted to strike in the Central Highlands in 1975. In Saigon the answer was received at the same moment and in the same words, and it fell on an army whose defence of every besieged town had been built for a decade around the aircraft that would not come.

In this war the defence of Phuoc Binh had more rounds and a radio to the end, and neither reached the reasons it fell. The province's ammunition point held about a third more 105mm rounds than history's, most of them from Bien Hoa, and the Regional Force battalions' posts in the province reported on the air until they were overrun, because their batteries were fresh. The PAVN's 130mm guns and its T-54s decided the siege, as they had historically: the province's two 155mm and four 105mm howitzers were silenced by counter-battery fire in the first week, and the rounds that would have fed them were still in the ammunition point when the 7th Division took it²⁰. What absorbed the difference was the decision of 18 December not to send a reserve and the PAVN's artillery, which no rounds for 105mm guns could answer. One thing went to Hanoi that had not gone historically. The 4th Corps' artillery staff reported that the ARVN's guns had fired in the first week at a rate the General Staff's estimate of the 1974 ration did not allow, and the B-2 Front's intelligence section, asked where the rounds came from, answered with the name of the Bien Hoa arsenal and the tonnage of propellant the port of Saigon had landed for it in 1974⁸. It was the first time the North's planners counted the Republic's own industry as part of its strength.

### Changed: The Politburo's calendar: Saigon before the rains
*25 Mar – 14 Apr 1975 · Hanoi and the roads south · EVMT01-4*

*Initiative: enemy*

The date of the fall of Saigon was set in Hanoi between 25 March and 14 April, and it was set by the rains and by the road. On 25 March, with Hue abandoned and the Highlands column destroyed, the Politburo resolved to take Saigon before the rainy season, which in the southern provinces begins in May and turns the lowlands around the capital to mud; on 31 March, with Da Nang taken, it decided to do it in April; and on 14 April it named the operation the Ho Chi Minh Campaign. Between those dates the whole of the PAVN's effort went into moving its corps to the capital: the 1st Corps, the strategic reserve, was brought south from the North by road, a march of more than 1,500 kilometres, and reached its assembly areas north of Saigon only in the third week of April; the 2nd Corps came down the coast behind the collapse of I and II Corps; and the 3rd and 4th Corps closed from the Highlands and the east²¹. General Van Tien Dung's plan set the assault for the last days of April because that was when the last corps would be in place and the first rains still a fortnight off.

In this war the inputs to that plan were different in three places and the plan was not. Dung's staff knew from the prisoners of Duc Duc and the reports of 1974 that the ARVN's battalions were better led than in 1972, and from the first three days at Xuan Loc that the 18th Division's squads could stop an assault battalion at 400 metres. It drew the conclusion it had drawn at every stage of the war, and it drew it faster: a well-led ARVN division is to be bypassed and isolated, not assaulted, and the assault is kept for the moment when the defence has nothing behind it. In the Delta the Front was weaker than history's, and Group 232's task of cutting Route 4 to the south of the capital fell more to PAVN regiments and less to the Front's local forces; it was done on the historical day. And the 7th and 9th Divisions, with the green companies of 1972's losses, were given the roles in which greenness cost least¹⁸.

None of the three reached the critical path. The date of 30 April was the product of the march of the 1st Corps and of a resolution to finish before the rains, and nothing the reforms had built in the ARVN stood on the road from Thanh Hoa to Binh Duong. A delay of a few days at Xuan Loc or Phan Rang was absorbed by a plan that was waiting for its last corps anyway; only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps, enough to keep the 1st Corps' road or the coast closed into May, would have put the assault into the rains and forced Hanoi to choose between fighting in the mud and waiting for the dry season of 1976¹⁸. That delay was in the hands of the President who gave the orders of 13 and 14 March, and of nobody the reforms had chosen.

The arsenal and the battery works were the first provision since the baseline to reach the Republic's sustainment after 1973, and they were tested against this critical path in the same terms. They did not reach it either. Ban Me Thuot fell on 10–12 March to a concentration Phu had not seen and a surprise no ammunition answers. The orders of 13 and 14 March rested on three of Thieu's judgments: that the United States would not return, that the army had no reserve while the Airborne and the Marines were tied to I Corps, and that the aid then voted would not let him hold the whole country. The base touched only the third, and only in part, since it stretched the rounds and not the fuel, the aircraft or the divisions; a President who could not hold Pleiku with the Airborne in Quang Tri could not hold it with more 105mm rounds either. The collapse of I Corps was a collapse of families on the road, and no factory reached that. Where the base did act in March and April, it acted on fights already off the path: the 18th Division at Xuan Loc and the 25th at Cu Chi drew from Long Binh and Bien Hoa with batteries for every set, and Hoang Cam went round them. The test leaves the delay in the collapse of I and II Corps at a few days at most, against the three weeks that would have put the assault into the rains⁸. The date of 30 April stands, derived again and not carried.

The base did change one line of Dung's plan. After Phuoc Long the General Staff counted the Bien Hoa works as part of the Republic's strength, and the order to the 4th Corps for the final assault named the arsenal, the steelworks and the Go Vap plant among the objectives to be taken intact rather than shelled, on the Politburo's instruction that the South's industry be preserved for the reunified country⁸. It changed whose the plants would be. It did not change the day.

### Changed: The fall of Saigon
*29–30 Apr 1975 · Saigon · EV000-98*

*Initiative: enemy*
By late April five PAVN corps, Group 232 and the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Corps, with 15 infantry divisions and three tank regiments, encircled Saigon in the Ho Chi Minh Campaign. Rockets and artillery hit Tan Son Nhut on the morning of 29 April; two US Marine guards, Corporal Charles McMahon and Lance Corporal Darwin Judge, were killed, the last American servicemen killed in action in Vietnam. At 10:51 Operation Frequent Wind began: Marine and Air Force helicopters lifted 395 Americans and more than 4,000 Vietnamese from the Defense Attaché Office compound, and 978 Americans and about 1,100 Vietnamese from the embassy roof and grounds, to the ships of the Seventh Fleet. Ambassador Graham Martin left on a helicopter at 04:58 on 30 April²². Thousands of Vietnamese who had worked with the Americans were left behind.

At 10:24 on 30 April Minh announced an unconditional surrender. PAVN tanks crashed through the gates of the Presidential Palace, Tank 390 through the main gate, and at 11:30 a soldier raised the flag of the Front over the palace²². The Republic of Vietnam had ceased to exist. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City; Vietnam was formally reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976.

In this war the Central Intelligence Organization's building held the national Phung Hoang file, about 240,000 names with photographs and fingerprints for about 90,000, consolidated there since 1971. The destruction plan for the building required the order of the Director General of the CIO, who left by the embassy's helicopters on 29 April; a section chief and two clerks burned the index and part of the photographic file in the building's courtyard on the morning of the 30th and were arrested in it that afternoon. The PAVN's security troops, with the Ministry of the Interior's southern section behind them, had the rest of the file by evening. It is not possible to say how many of the men and women sent to re-education camps after 1975, or kept there longest, were sent because their names were in it; the camps' own records are not available, and the victors had other lists⁶. It is possible to say that the file held the names of every informant, centre officer, PRU member, Chieu Hoi rallier and selected adviser's counterpart of eleven years, that it was the most complete record of the Republic's friends the war produced, and that this headquarters built it.

In this war the 4th Corps' columns reached the Bien Hoa industrial zone on the morning of 30 April with orders to take it intact, and they did. The Directorate's general had left on the 28th; the plant managers and about two hundred of the engineers stayed, most of them because they did not believe the new government would want them less than the old one had. The arsenal's stores held about 40 million cartridges and about 90,000 105mm rounds, loaded and unissued, the last of what the 1974 propellant had made, and the battery works held about 300,000 dry cells. Within a month the works were running under a military management board of the Ministry of Heavy Industry, and the case lines made cartridges for the PAVN's captured M16s and M4A1s⁸. The Republic's own industry, built to stretch its last aid dollar, became the victors' largest workshop in the South on the day the Republic ended, and that, too, this headquarters built.
